title: 'Crazy Jimmy' died as he lived: Gang leader Hoang felled in hail of bullets, inquiry told
article: Notorious gang leader Long Duy "Crazy Jimmy" Hoang died as violently as he lived, mowed down in a barrage of police bullets after shooting at an officer trying to arrest him.

Three members of the police tactical unit, two carrying submachine guns and one with a semi-automatic rifle, fired 30 rounds at Hoang on Jan. 5, 2000, as he sat in the driver's seat of the Honda Accord he'd crashed to a stop, witnesses told a fatality inquiry on Monday.

The leader of the Crazy Jimmy gang had hit a parked car near 148th Street and 89th Avenue around 8 p.m. after police chased him at speeds of up to 100 km/h, following reports linking him to an armed home invasion.
Passenger Hoa Tran jumped out and surrendered, but members of the tactical unit approached the Accord cautiously.

Const. Randall Loxterkamp could see Hoang -- lab tests later showed he'd been using cocaine -- fumbling for something under his seat even as the officer shouted from the car's passenger side to put his hands up.
"At that time the driver pulled up a handgun. I started to yell 'Gun, gun, gun' to let my other members around know that," Loxterkamp testified Monday.
"As soon as the gun came up and I saw it pointed (at me), I started to move, and I heard it shoot almost immediately."
Loxterkamp heard the Glock pistol, similar to ones carried by police, go off once or twice.
From the front of the car, he fired bursts from his MP5 submachine-gun through the windshield at the 28-year-old Hoang.
Loxterkamp discharged 18 shots in a couple of seconds before deciding the situation was safe.
"Where I was shooting, I could see that the threat had stopped: the gun had gone down; there wasn't really any movement."
Two other members of the tactical unit heard the Glock discharged and, fearing their colleague's life was in danger, opened fire on Hoang as well.
Const. Robin Jorritsma blasted 10 submachine-gun rounds through the rear window, while Const. Freddie Blondel fired two semi- automatic rifle rounds from the passenger side.
They'd been briefed earlier that night on Hoang's dangerous reputation, Blondel said.
"He had in recent weeks been making threats that he wanted to be in a confrontation with police in order to elevate his standing among his peers in his gang," said the 16-year police veteran.

"He was the ringleader of an Asian gang that was heavily involved in the distribution of drugs. As well, he and his associates had been involved in numerous violent incidents ... including firearms and drive-by shootings."
The incident ended within seconds, before a sergeant called "Cease fire," Blondel said.
Carrying a bulletproof shield, officers then went to the car and removed the injured man's gun.
His seat-belt was cut and he was moved to the ground so Loxterkamp, a former emergency medical worker, could give first aid until an ambulance arrived.
"I found a number of holes in his chest and shoulder area, and one in the right temple."
No police officers were injured.
Chief provincial medical examiner Dr. Graeme Dowling testified the shot to the temple was Hoang's most serious injury.
He died in hospital two days later.
The doctor pulled nine bullets from Hoang's corpse, which was hit in the head, chest, both arms and the right leg.
However, the dead man may have been shot up to 16 times, Dowling said.
The fatality inquiry is set to last for the rest of the week. Hoang's passenger Tran, who wasn't charged in connection with the shooting, is scheduled to testify today.
